title: Inner Product Space
content:
Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$). An
inner product on $V$ is a function that assigns to every
pair of vectors $u,v \in V$ a scalar $\langle u,v \rangle$
satisfying the following axioms for all $u,v,w \in V$ and
$k \in \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$):

1. $\langle u+v,\ w \rangle = \langle u,w \rangle+\langle v,w \rangle$ \hfill (linearity in first slot)
2. $\langle ku,\ v \rangle = k\langle u,v \rangle$ \hfill (homogeneity)
3. $\langle u,v \rangle = \overline{\langle v,u \rangle}$ \hfill (conjugate symmetry; $=\langle v,u \rangle$ over $\mathbb{R}$)
4. $\langle u,u \rangle \ge 0$, and $\langle u,u \rangle = 0$ if
        and only if $u=0$ \hfill (positive definiteness)

A vector space $V$ equipped with an inner product is called an
inner product space. The norm (length) of a
vector $u$ is defined as
\[
\|u\| = \sqrt{\langle u,u \rangle}.
\]
A vector $u$ with $\|u\|=1$ is called a unit vector, and
the process of replacing $u$ with $u/\|u\|$ is called
normalization.

title: Example 5.1 --- The Standard Inner Product on \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{R
content:
^n$}{Rn}}
Let $u=(1,-2,3)$ and $v=(4,0,-1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Using the
standard (Euclidean) inner product
$\langle u,v \rangle = u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3$, compute
$\langle u,v \rangle$.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = (1)(4)+(-2)(0)+(3)(-1) = 4+0-3 = 1.
\]
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = \boxed{1}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.2 --- Computing a Norm
content:
Find $\|u\|$ for $u=(1,-5,3)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ using the standard
inner product.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,u \rangle = 1^2+(-5)^2+3^2 = 1+25+9 = 35.
\]
\[
\|u\| = \sqrt{35}
\]
\[
\|u\| = \boxed{\sqrt{35}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.3 --- Past Paper 2024 Q1(xii) \& 2025 Q1(x)
content:
Normalize the vector $v=(1,2,4,5)$.

Solution:
First compute the norm:
\[
\|v\| = \sqrt{1^2+2^2+4^2+5^2} = \sqrt{1+4+16+25} = \sqrt{46}.
\]
The normalized (unit) vector is obtained by dividing each component
by $\|v\|$:
\[
\hat{v} = \frac{v}{\|v\|} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{46}},\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{46}},\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{46}},\
\frac{5}{\sqrt{46}}\right).
\]
Verification: $\|\hat{v}\|^2 =
\dfrac{1+4+16+25}{46}=\dfrac{46}{46}=1$. ✓
\[
\hat{v} = \boxed{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{46}},\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{46}},\
\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{46}},\ \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{46}}\right)}
\]

title: Properties of the Inner Product
content:
1. $\langle u,\ v+w \rangle = \langle u,v \rangle+\langle u,w \rangle$ \hfill (linearity in second slot, over $\mathbb{R}$)
2. $\langle u,\ kv \rangle = k\langle u,v \rangle$ over
        $\mathbb{R}$; $\langle u,\ kv \rangle = \overline{k}\langle u,v \rangle$
        over $\mathbb{C}$ \hfill (conjugate-homogeneity in second slot)
3. $\langle 0,\ v \rangle = \langle v,\ 0 \rangle = 0$ for
        every $v \in V$ \hfill (zero vector property)
4. $\|kv\| = |k|\,\|v\|$ for any scalar $k$ \hfill (norm scaling)
5. $\|u\| \ge 0$, with $\|u\|=0$ if and only if $u=0$ \hfill (positive definiteness of norm)

title: Weighted Inner Product on \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{R
content:
^n$}{Rn}}
Given fixed positive weights $w_1,w_2,\dots,w_n$, the function
�MATH0�
defines a valid inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$, called a
weighted Euclidean inner product. Choosing all weights
equal to $1$ recovers the standard (unweighted) inner product.

title: Example 5.4 --- Computing a Weighted Inner Product
content:
Let $u=(1,2)$ and $v=(3,-1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with weights
$w_1=2$ and $w_2=5$. Compute $\langle u,v \rangle$ using this
weighted inner product.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = w_1u_1v_1+w_2u_2v_2 = 2(1)(3)+5(2)(-1) = 6-10 = -4.
\]
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = \boxed{-4}
\]

\subsection*{Complex Inner Product Space \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{C}^n$}{Cn}}

title: Standard Inner Product on \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{C
content:
^n$}{Cn}}
For $u=(u_1,\dots,u_n)$ and $v=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ in $\mathbb{C}^n$,
the standard inner product is defined using complex conjugates to
guarantee $\langle u,u \rangle \ge 0$:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = u_1\overline{v_1}+u_2\overline{v_2}+\cdots+u_n\overline{v_n}.
\]

title: Example 5.5 --- Inner Product in \texorpdfstring{$\mathbb{C
content:
^2$}{C2}}
Let $u=(2+i,\ 1-i)$ and $v=(1,\ 2+i)$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$. Compute
$\langle u,v \rangle$.

Solution:
$$\begin{align*}
\langle u,v \rangle &= (2+i)\overline{(1)}+(1-i)\overline{(2+i)}\\
&= (2+i)(1)+(1-i)(2-i)\\
&= (2+i)+\big(2-i-2i+i^2\big)\\
&= (2+i)+(2-3i-1)\\
&= (2+i)+(1-3i)\\
&= 3-2i.
\end{align*}$$
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = \boxed{3-2i}
\]

\subsection*{Function Space Inner Product}

title: Inner Product on a Function Space
content:
Let $V=C[a,b]$ be the vector space of continuous real functions on
the interval $[a,b]$. The function
\[
\langle f,g \rangle = \int_a^b f(t)g(t)\,dt
\]
defines an inner product on $C[a,b]$.

title: Example 5.6 --- Inner Product of Functions
content:
Let $f(t)=t$ and $g(t)=t^2$ in $C[0,1]$. Compute
$\langle f,g \rangle$ using $\langle f,g \rangle=\int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,dt$.

Solution:
\[
\langle f,g \rangle = \int_0^1 t \cdot t^2 \,dt = \int_0^1 t^3\,dt
= \left[\frac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{4}-0 = \frac{1}{4}.
\]
\[
\langle f,g \rangle = \boxed{\dfrac{1}{4}}
\]

\subsection*{Matrix Space Inner Product}

title: Inner Product on \texorpdfstring{$M_{m,n
content:
$}{Mmn}}
For matrices $A,B \in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{R})$, the function
�MATH0�
defines an inner product on $M_{m,n}$, where $\operatorname{tr}$
denotes the trace (sum of diagonal entries). This is equivalent to

title: Example 5.7 --- Inner Product of Matrices
content:
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$ and
$B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$ in $M_{2,2}$. Compute
$\langle A,B \rangle$.

Solution:
Sum the products of corresponding entries:
\[
\langle A,B \rangle = (1)(2)+(2)(1)+(0)(3)+(-1)(4) = 2+2+0-4 = 0.
\]
\[
\langle A,B \rangle = \boxed{0}
\]

title: {Common Inner Product Spaces to Remember:}
content:
Common Inner Product Spaces to Remember:

1. $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the standard (Euclidean) inner product
        $\langle u,v \rangle = \sum u_iv_i$
2. $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a weighted inner product
        $\langle u,v \rangle = \sum w_iu_iv_i$, $w_i>0$
3. $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\langle u,v \rangle = \sum u_i\overline{v_i}$
        (conjugate on the second vector)
4. $C[a,b]$ with $\langle f,g \rangle = \int_a^b f(t)g(t)\,dt$
5. $M_{m,n}$ with $\langle A,B \rangle = \operatorname{tr}(B^TA)$
        (sum of products of corresponding entries)
6. When $\langle u,v \rangle=0$ for two nonzero vectors, they
        are called orthogonal (covered in Section 5.5).

title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
content:
Let $u,v$ be vectors in an inner product space $V$. Then:
\[
|\langle u,v \rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent
(one is a scalar multiple of the other).

title: Triangle Inequality
content:
Let $u,v$ be vectors in an inner product space $V$. Then:
\[
\|u+v\| \le \|u\|+\|v\|.
\]
This is also called Minkowski's Inequality and follows
directly from the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality.

title: Example 5.8 --- Past Paper 2023 Q1(i)
content:
If $V$ is an inner product space and $u,v \in V$, show that
\[
\cos\theta = \frac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}.
\]

Solution:
By the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, $|\langle u,v \rangle| \le
\|u\|\,\|v\|$ for all nonzero $u,v \in V$. Dividing both sides by
$\|u\|\,\|v\|>0$:
\[
-1 \le \frac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|} \le 1.
\]
Since the quantity $\dfrac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}$ always
lies in $[-1,1]$, it is a valid value for the cosine of some angle
$\theta$ with $0 \le \theta \le \pi$. This angle is defined to be
the angle between $u$ and $v$, giving:
\[
\cos\theta = \boxed{\frac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}}
\]
\hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.9 --- Past Paper 2021 Q1(i)
content:
Compute the angle between vectors $u=(-1,1,2)$ and $v=(2,1,-1)$.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = (-1)(2)+(1)(1)+(2)(-1) = -2+1-2 = -3.
\]
\[
\|u\| = \sqrt{(-1)^2+1^2+2^2} = \sqrt{6}, \qquad
\|v\| = \sqrt{2^2+1^2+(-1)^2} = \sqrt{6}.
\]
\[
\cos\theta = \frac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|} =
\frac{-3}{\sqrt{6}\cdot\sqrt{6}} = \frac{-3}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}.
\]
\[
\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]
\[
\theta = \boxed{120^\circ}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.10 --- Verifying the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
content:
Verify the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality for $u=(1,2,3)$ and
$v=(4,-1,2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = (1)(4)+(2)(-1)+(3)(2) = 4-2+6 = 8.
\]
\[
|\langle u,v \rangle| = 8.
\]
\[
\|u\| = \sqrt{1+4+9} = \sqrt{14}, \qquad \|v\| = \sqrt{16+1+4} = \sqrt{21}.
\]
\[
\|u\|\,\|v\| = \sqrt{14}\cdot\sqrt{21} = \sqrt{294} \approx 17.15.
\]
Since $8 \le 17.15$:
\[
|\langle u,v \rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\| \quad\checkmark
\]
The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality holds. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.11 --- Verifying the Triangle Inequality
content:
Verify the Triangle Inequality for $u=(3,0,4)$ and $v=(1,2,2)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
\[
u+v = (4,2,6).
\]
\[
\|u+v\| = \sqrt{4^2+2^2+6^2} = \sqrt{16+4+36} = \sqrt{56} \approx 7.48.
\]
\[
\|u\| = \sqrt{9+0+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5, \qquad \|v\| = \sqrt{1+4+4} = \sqrt{9} = 3.
\]
\[
\|u\|+\|v\| = 5+3 = 8.
\]
Since $7.48 \le 8$:
\[
\|u+v\| \le \|u\|+\|v\| \quad\checkmark
\]
The Triangle Inequality holds. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.12 --- Past Paper 2021 Q1(xii)
content:
Find the norm of $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{4},\dfrac{1}{3},\dfrac{1}{6}\right)
\in \mathbb{R}^4$ with respect to the Euclidean inner product on
$\mathbb{R}^4$.

Solution:
\[
\|v\|^2 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2+\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2
= \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{36}.
\]
Using the common denominator $144$:
\[
\|v\|^2 = \frac{36}{144}+\frac{9}{144}+\frac{16}{144}+\frac{4}{144} = \frac{65}{144}.
\]
\[
\|v\| = \sqrt{\frac{65}{144}} = \frac{\sqrt{65}}{12}
\]
\[
\|v\| = \boxed{\dfrac{\sqrt{65}}{12}}
\]

title: {Cauchy-Schwarz --- Key Facts:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Cauchy-Schwarz
content:
Cauchy-Schwarz --- Key Facts:

1. Cauchy-Schwarz guarantees $\dfrac{\langle u,v \rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|}
        \in [-1,1]$, which is what makes the angle formula
        well-defined.
2. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz occurs exactly when $u,v$ are
        parallel (one is a scalar multiple of the other).
3. $\theta=90^\circ$ (i.e. $\cos\theta=0$) exactly when
        $\langle u,v \rangle=0$ --- this is the definition of
        orthogonality, covered next.
4. Always compute $\langle u,v \rangle$, $\|u\|$, and $\|v\|$
        separately before substituting into the cosine formula, to
        avoid arithmetic errors.

title: Orthogonal Vectors and Orthogonal Complement
content:
Vectors $u,v$ in an inner product space $V$ are called
orthogonal if $\langle u,v \rangle=0$. For a subset
$S \subseteq V$, the orthogonal complement of $S$, denoted
$S^{\perp}$, is the set of all vectors in $V$ orthogonal to every
vector in $S$:
\[
S^{\perp} = \{v \in V : \langle v,s \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } s \in S\}.
\]
$S^{\perp}$ is always a subspace of $V$, even if $S$ itself is not.

title: Example 5.13 --- Checking Orthogonality
content:
Determine whether $u=(2,-1,3)$ and $v=(1,5,1)$ are orthogonal in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
\[
\langle u,v \rangle = (2)(1)+(-1)(5)+(3)(1) = 2-5+3 = 0.
\]
Since $\langle u,v \rangle=0$, the vectors are
orthogonal. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.14 --- Past Paper 2023 Q1(xii)
content:
Find a vector orthogonal to $u_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix}$
and $u_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\-4\end{bmatrix}$.

Solution:
A vector orthogonal to both $u_1$ and $u_2$ can be found using the
cross product $u_1 \times u_2$:
\[
u_1 \times u_2 =
\begin{vmatrix}
\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k}\\
1 & 2 & 1\\
2 & 1 & -4
\end{vmatrix}
\]
$$$$\begin{align*}
&= \mathbf{i}\big((2)(-4)-(1)(1)\big) - \mathbf{j}\big((1)(-4)-(1)(2)\big) + \mathbf{k}\big((1)(1)-(2)(2)\big)\\
&= \mathbf{i}(-8-1) - \mathbf{j}(-4-2) + \mathbf{k}(1-4)\\
&= -9\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}.
\end{align*}$$$$
So $w=(-9,6,-3)$, or dividing by $-3$, the simplified vector
$w=(3,-2,1)$.

Verification: $\langle u_1,w \rangle = 3-4+1=0$. ✓\quad
$\langle u_2,w \rangle = 6-2-4=0$. ✓
\[
w = \boxed{(3,\ -2,\ 1)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.15 --- Finding an Orthogonal Complement
content:
Find $W^{\perp}$ where $W=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0)\}$ in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
We need all $(x,y,z)$ such that $\langle (x,y,z),(1,1,0) \rangle=0$:
\[
x+y = 0 \implies y=-x, \quad z \text{ free}.
\]
So every vector in $W^{\perp}$ has the form
$(x,-x,z) = x(1,-1,0)+z(0,0,1)$.
\[
W^{\perp} = \boxed{\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,0),\ (0,0,1)\}}, \qquad \dim(W^{\perp})=2
\]

\subsection*{Orthogonal Matrices}

title: Orthogonal Matrix
content:
A real square matrix $P$ is called orthogonal if
\[
P^TP = PP^T = I,
\]
equivalently, $P^{-1}=P^T$. This holds if and only if the rows of
$P$ (and equivalently the columns of $P$) form an orthonormal set of
vectors.

title: Example 5.16 --- Verifying an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Show that
$P=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{3}{5}&\tfrac{4}{5}\\-\tfrac{4}{5}&\tfrac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}$
is an orthogonal matrix.

Solution:
Compute $P^TP$:
\[
P^T = \begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{3}{5}&-\tfrac{4}{5}\\\tfrac{4}{5}&\tfrac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
P^TP = \begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{3}{5}&-\tfrac{4}{5}\\\tfrac{4}{5}&\tfrac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{3}{5}&\tfrac{4}{5}\\-\tfrac{4}{5}&\tfrac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}\tfrac{9}{25}+\tfrac{16}{25}&\tfrac{12}{25}-\tfrac{12}{25}\\\tfrac{12}{25}-\tfrac{12}{25}&\tfrac{16}{25}+\tfrac{9}{25}\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = I.
\]
Since $P^TP=I$, $P$ is an orthogonal matrix. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.17 --- Past Paper 2021 Q1(xi)
content:
If $A$ is an orthogonal matrix, show that $\det A = 1$ or $-1$.

Solution:
Since $A$ is orthogonal, $A^TA=I$. Taking the determinant of both
sides:
\[
\det(A^TA) = \det(I) = 1.
\]
Using the property $\det(A^TA)=\det(A^T)\det(A)$ and
$\det(A^T)=\det(A)$:
\[
\det(A)\cdot\det(A) = 1 \implies (\det A)^2 = 1.
\]
Taking the square root of both sides:
\[
\det A = \pm 1
\]
\hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.18 --- Past Paper 2024 Q1(vii) \& 2025 Q1(vi)
content:
Show that matrix $P$ is orthogonal if and only if $P^T$ is
orthogonal.

Solution:
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $P$ is orthogonal. Then
$P^TP=PP^T=I$. We must show $(P^T)^TP^T=P^T(P^T)^T=I$. Since
$(P^T)^T=P$, this becomes:
\[
(P^T)^TP^T = PP^T = I \quad\checkmark
\]
\[
P^T(P^T)^T = P^TP = I \quad\checkmark
\]
So $P^T$ is orthogonal.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $P^T$ is orthogonal. Then by the same
argument applied to $P^T$ in place of $P$:
\[
(P^T)^TP^T = I \implies PP^T = I \quad\checkmark
\]
\[
P^T(P^T)^T = I \implies P^TP = I \quad\checkmark
\]
So $P$ is orthogonal.

Since each condition implies the other, $P$ is orthogonal if and
only if $P^T$ is orthogonal. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.19 --- Past Paper 2023 Q1(xi)
content:
Find an orthogonal matrix whose first row is
$\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$.

Solution:
For a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix, the second row must be a unit
vector orthogonal to the first row. A vector orthogonal to
$\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$ is obtained by
swapping components and negating one:
$\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}},\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)$.

Check unit length: $\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2+
\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{4}{5}+\dfrac{1}{5}=1$. ✓

Check orthogonality with row 1:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left(-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\right)+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\right)
= -\dfrac{2}{5}+\dfrac{2}{5}=0$. ✓
\[
P = \boxed{\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}&\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\\[4pt]-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}&\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\end{bmatrix}}
\]

title: Properties of Orthogonal Matrices
content:
1. $P^{-1}=P^T$ \hfill (inverse equals transpose)
2. $\det P = \pm 1$ \hfill (determinant restriction)
3. The rows of $P$ form an orthonormal set, and so do the
        columns of $P$ \hfill (orthonormal rows and columns)
4. $P$ is orthogonal if and only if $P^T$ is orthogonal \hfill (transpose symmetry)
5. The product of two orthogonal matrices is orthogonal \hfill (closure under multiplication)

title: {Orthogonality --- Exam Strategy:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] To
content:
Orthogonality --- Exam Strategy:

1. To test orthogonality of two vectors, simply check whether
        $\langle u,v \rangle=0$.
2. To find a vector orthogonal to two given vectors in
        $\mathbb{R}^3$, use the cross product.
3. To verify a matrix is orthogonal, check $P^TP=I$ (it is
        enough to check one of $P^TP=I$ or $PP^T=I$ for a square
        matrix).
4. Building an orthogonal matrix from a given row/column: each
        remaining row/column must be a unit vector orthogonal to
        all previously chosen rows/columns.

title: Orthogonal and Orthonormal Sets
content:
A set $S=\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\}$ of nonzero vectors in an
inner product space $V$ is called an orthogonal set if every
pair of distinct vectors in $S$ is orthogonal:
\[
\langle v_i,v_j \rangle = 0 \qquad \text{for all } i \neq j.
\]
If, in addition, every vector in $S$ has norm $1$ (i.e.
$\|v_i\|=1$ for all $i$), then $S$ is called an
orthonormal set. Any orthogonal set can be converted into
an orthonormal set by normalizing each vector (dividing it
by its own norm).

title: Example 5.20 --- Verifying an Orthogonal Set
content:
Show that $S=\{(1,1,1),\ (1,-2,1),\ (1,0,-1)\}$ is an orthogonal set
in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
Label the vectors $v_1=(1,1,1)$, $v_2=(1,-2,1)$, $v_3=(1,0,-1)$, and
check all three pairwise inner products:
\[
\langle v_1,v_2 \rangle = (1)(1)+(1)(-2)+(1)(1) = 1-2+1 = 0.
\]
\[
\langle v_1,v_3 \rangle = (1)(1)+(1)(0)+(1)(-1) = 1+0-1 = 0.
\]
\[
\langle v_2,v_3 \rangle = (1)(1)+(-2)(0)+(1)(-1) = 1+0-1 = 0.
\]
Since all pairwise inner products are zero, $S$ is an
orthogonal set. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.21 --- Converting to an Orthonormal Set
content:
Convert the orthogonal set from Example 5.20 into an orthonormal
set.

Solution:
Compute the norm of each vector:
\[
\|v_1\| = \sqrt{1+1+1} = \sqrt{3}, \qquad
\|v_2\| = \sqrt{1+4+1} = \sqrt{6}, \qquad
\|v_3\| = \sqrt{1+0+1} = \sqrt{2}.
\]
Divide each vector by its own norm:
\[
q_1 = \frac{v_1}{\|v_1\|} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right), \qquad
q_2 = \frac{v_2}{\|v_2\|} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt6},\frac{-2}{\sqrt6},\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\right),
\]
\[
q_3 = \frac{v_3}{\|v_3\|} = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt2},0,\frac{-1}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]
\[
\{q_1,q_2,q_3\} = \boxed{\left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right),
\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{-2}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right),
\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0,\tfrac{-1}{\sqrt2}\right)\right\}}
\]

title: Orthogonal Sets Are Linearly Independent
content:
Every orthogonal set of nonzero vectors in an inner product space
$V$ is linearly independent.

title: Example 5.22 --- Proving the Independence of Orthogonal Sets
content:
Prove that an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors
$\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\}$ is linearly independent.

Solution:
Suppose $a_1v_1+a_2v_2+\cdots+a_nv_n = 0$. Take the inner product of
both sides with $v_i$ (for a fixed but arbitrary index $i$):
\[
\left\langle \sum_{j=1}^n a_jv_j,\ v_i \right\rangle = \langle 0,v_i \rangle = 0.
\]
By linearity of the inner product:
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\langle v_j,v_i \rangle = 0.
\]
Since $S$ is orthogonal, $\langle v_j,v_i \rangle = 0$ for every
$j \neq i$, so all terms vanish except the $j=i$ term:
\[
a_i\langle v_i,v_i \rangle = 0.
\]
Since $v_i$ is nonzero, $\langle v_i,v_i \rangle = \|v_i\|^2 \neq
0$. Therefore $a_i=0$.

Since $i$ was arbitrary, $a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n=0$, which is the
trivial solution. Hence $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ is linearly
independent. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 5.23 --- Orthogonal Set as a Basis
content:
Using the result of Example 5.22, explain why the orthogonal set
$S=\{(1,1,1),(1,-2,1),(1,0,-1)\}$ from Example 5.20 is a basis of
$\mathbb{R}^3$.

Solution:
By Example 5.22, an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is always
linearly independent. Since $S$ consists of $3$ nonzero orthogonal
vectors, $S$ is linearly independent.

Since $\dim(\mathbb{R}^3)=3$ and $S$ contains exactly $3$
independent vectors, $S$ automatically spans $\mathbb{R}^3$ as
well. Hence:
\[
S \ \boxed{\text{is a basis of } \mathbb{R}^3}
\]
(In fact, $S$ is called an orthogonal basis of
$\mathbb{R}^3$.) \hfill$\square$

title: Orthogonal Basis and Fourier Coefficients
content:
An orthogonal basis of a vector space $V$ is a basis that
is also an orthogonal set. If $S=\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\}$ is an
orthogonal basis of $V$, every vector $v \in V$ can be written as:
\[
v = c_1v_1+c_2v_2+\cdots+c_nv_n, \qquad \text{where }
c_i = \frac{\langle v,v_i \rangle}{\langle v_i,v_i \rangle} = \frac{\langle v,v_i \rangle}{\|v_i\|^2}.
\]
The scalars $c_i$ are called the Fourier coefficients of
$v$ relative to $S$. If $S$ is instead an orthonormal
basis, the formula simplifies (since $\|v_i\|=1$) to:
\[
v = \langle v,v_1 \rangle v_1+\langle v,v_2 \rangle v_2+\cdots+\langle v,v_n \rangle v_n.
\]

title: Example 5.24 --- Fourier Coefficients Relative to an Orthogonal Basis
content:
Express $v=(2,3,-1)$ as a linear combination of the orthogonal basis
$S=\{(1,1,1),(1,-2,1),(1,0,-1)\}$ using Fourier coefficients.

Solution:
Compute each Fourier coefficient $c_i = \dfrac{\langle v,v_i
\rangle}{\|v_i\|^2}$, reusing $\|v_1\|^2=3$, $\|v_2\|^2=6$,
$\|v_3\|^2=2$ from Example 5.21:
\[
\langle v,v_1 \rangle = 2+3-1 = 4, \qquad c_1 = \frac{4}{3}.
\]
\[
\langle v,v_2 \rangle = 2-6-1 = -5, \qquad c_2 = \frac{-5}{6}.
\]
\[
\langle v,v_3 \rangle = 2+0+1 = 3, \qquad c_3 = \frac{3}{2}.
\]
Verification:
$$$$\begin{align*}
c_1v_1+c_2v_2+c_3v_3
&= \tfrac{4}{3}(1,1,1)+\left(-\tfrac{5}{6}\right)(1,-2,1)+\tfrac{3}{2}(1,0,-1)\\
&= \left(\tfrac{8}{6}-\tfrac{5}{6}+\tfrac{9}{6},\ \tfrac{8}{6}+\tfrac{10}{6}+0,\ \tfrac{8}{6}-\tfrac{5}{6}-\tfrac{9}{6}\right)\\
&= \left(\tfrac{12}{6},\ \tfrac{18}{6},\ \tfrac{-6}{6}\right) = (2,3,-1) = v. \quad\checkmark
\end{align*}$$$$
\[
v = \boxed{\tfrac{4}{3}v_1 - \tfrac{5}{6}v_2 + \tfrac{3}{2}v_3}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.25 --- Coordinates Relative to an Orthonormal Basis
content:
Express $v=(2,3,-1)$ in terms of the orthonormal basis
$\{q_1,q_2,q_3\}$ from Example 5.21.

Solution:
For an orthonormal basis, the coefficients are simply
$\langle v,q_i \rangle$ (no division by $\|v_i\|^2$ needed):
\[
\langle v,q_1 \rangle = \frac{2+3-1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}.
\]
\[
\langle v,q_2 \rangle = \frac{2-6-1}{\sqrt6} = \frac{-5}{\sqrt6}.
\]
\[
\langle v,q_3 \rangle = \frac{2+0+1}{\sqrt2} = \frac{3}{\sqrt2}.
\]
\[
v = \boxed{\tfrac{4}{\sqrt3}q_1 - \tfrac{5}{\sqrt6}q_2 + \tfrac{3}{\sqrt2}q_3}
\]
Notice these coefficients relate to the Fourier coefficients of
Example 5.24 by $c_i' = c_i\|v_i\|$ --- e.g.
$c_1\|v_1\| = \tfrac{4}{3}\cdot\sqrt3 = \tfrac{4}{\sqrt3}$.
✓ \hfill$\square$

title: Pythagorean Theorem
content:
If $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal vectors in an inner product space $V$,
then:
\[
\|u+v\|^2 = \|u\|^2+\|v\|^2.
\]

title: Example 5.26 --- Verifying the Pythagorean Theorem
content:
Verify the Pythagorean Theorem for the orthogonal vectors
$v_1=(1,1,1)$ and $v_2=(1,-2,1)$ from Example 5.20.

Solution:
\[
v_1+v_2 = (2,-1,2).
\]
\[
\|v_1+v_2\|^2 = 2^2+(-1)^2+2^2 = 4+1+4 = 9.
\]
\[
\|v_1\|^2 = 1+1+1 = 3, \qquad \|v_2\|^2 = 1+4+1 = 6.
\]
\[
\|v_1\|^2+\|v_2\|^2 = 3+6 = 9.
\]
Since $\|v_1+v_2\|^2 = 9 = \|v_1\|^2+\|v_2\|^2$, the Pythagorean
Theorem is verified. \hfill$\square$

title: {Orthogonal Sets and Bases --- Key
content:
Orthogonal Sets and Bases --- Key Facts:

1. An orthogonal set of nonzero vectors is automatically
        linearly independent --- no separate independence check is
        needed.
2. $n$ nonzero orthogonal vectors in an $n$-dimensional space
        automatically form an orthogonal basis.
3. Fourier coefficients avoid solving a linear system: once a
        basis is known to be orthogonal, each coefficient is found
        directly via $c_i=\dfrac{\langle v,v_i \rangle}{\|v_i\|^2}$.
4. For an orthonormal basis, the formula simplifies
        further to $c_i=\langle v,v_i \rangle$, since $\|v_i\|=1$.
5. The Pythagorean Theorem applies only when the two
        vectors are orthogonal --- it is a quick way to verify
        orthogonality was used/computed correctly.

title: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization Process
content:
Let $\{u_1,u_2,\dots,u_n\}$ be a basis of an inner product space
$V$. The Gram-Schmidt process constructs an
orthogonal basis $\{v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n\}$ of $V$ as
follows:
\[
v_1 = u_1,
\]
\[
v_2 = u_2 - \frac{\langle u_2,v_1 \rangle}{\langle v_1,v_1 \rangle}v_1,
\]
\[
v_3 = u_3 - \frac{\langle u_3,v_1 \rangle}{\langle v_1,v_1 \rangle}v_1
- \frac{\langle u_3,v_2 \rangle}{\langle v_2,v_2 \rangle}v_2,
\]
and in general, for each $k=1,\dots,n$:
\[
v_k = u_k - \sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\langle u_k,v_i \rangle}{\langle v_i,v_i \rangle}v_i.
\]
Each new vector $v_k$ is formed by subtracting from $u_k$ its
projections onto all previously constructed vectors
$v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}$. Normalizing each $v_i$ (dividing by
$\|v_i\|$) then produces an orthonormal basis
$\{q_1,q_2,\dots,q_n\}$ of $V$.

title: Existence of an Orthonormal Basis
content:
Every finite-dimensional inner product space $V$ has an orthogonal
basis, and hence also an orthonormal basis. Both can be obtained by
applying the Gram-Schmidt process to any basis of $V$.

title: Example 5.27 --- Gram-Schmidt Process for Two Vectors
content:
Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to $u_1=(3,4)$ and $u_2=(1,2)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^2$ to find an orthogonal basis, then normalize to find
an orthonormal basis.

Solution:
\[
v_1 = u_1 = (3,4).
\]
\[
\langle u_2,v_1 \rangle = (1)(3)+(2)(4) = 11, \qquad
\langle v_1,v_1 \rangle = 9+16 = 25.
\]
\[
v_2 = u_2 - \frac{11}{25}v_1 = (1,2) - \frac{11}{25}(3,4)
= \left(1-\frac{33}{25},\ 2-\frac{44}{25}\right)
= \left(-\frac{8}{25},\ \frac{6}{25}\right).
\]
Check: $\langle v_1,v_2 \rangle = 3\left(-\tfrac{8}{25}\right)+4\left(\tfrac{6}{25}\right)
= -\tfrac{24}{25}+\tfrac{24}{25}=0$. ✓

Normalize:
\[
\|v_1\| = \sqrt{9+16} = 5, \qquad
\|v_2\| = \sqrt{\tfrac{64}{625}+\tfrac{36}{625}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{100}{625}} = \frac{2}{5}.
\]
\[
q_1 = \frac{v_1}{\|v_1\|} = \left(\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right), \qquad
q_2 = \frac{v_2}{\|v_2\|} = \left(-\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}\right).
\]
\[
\{q_1,q_2\} = \boxed{\left\{\left(\tfrac{3}{5},\tfrac{4}{5}\right),\ \left(-\tfrac{4}{5},\tfrac{3}{5}\right)\right\}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.28 --- Past Paper 2024 Q3(b) \& 2025 Q3(b)
content:
Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to the basis vectors
$u_1=(1,1,1)$, $u_2=(0,1,1)$, $u_3=(0,0,1)$ to transform them into
an orthogonal basis, then normalize to obtain an orthonormal basis.

Solution:
\[
v_1 = u_1 = (1,1,1), \qquad \langle v_1,v_1 \rangle = 3.
\]
\[
\langle u_2,v_1 \rangle = 0+1+1 = 2.
\]
\[
v_2 = u_2 - \frac{2}{3}v_1 = (0,1,1)-\tfrac{2}{3}(1,1,1)
= \left(-\tfrac{2}{3},\ \tfrac{1}{3},\ \tfrac{1}{3}\right),
\qquad \langle v_2,v_2 \rangle = \tfrac{4}{9}+\tfrac{1}{9}+\tfrac{1}{9} = \tfrac{2}{3}.
\]
\[
\langle u_3,v_1 \rangle = 0+0+1 = 1, \qquad
\langle u_3,v_2 \rangle = 0+0+\tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{1}{3}.
\]
\[
v_3 = u_3 - \frac{1}{3}v_1 - \frac{1/3}{2/3}v_2
= (0,0,1) - \tfrac{1}{3}(1,1,1) - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(-\tfrac{2}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3}\right)
\]
\[
= (0,0,1) - \left(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3}\right) - \left(-\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{6}\right)
= \left(0,\ -\tfrac{1}{2},\ \tfrac{1}{2}\right).
\]
Check: $\langle v_1,v_3 \rangle=0-\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}=0$ ✓,\quad
$\langle v_2,v_3 \rangle=0-\tfrac{1}{6}+\tfrac{1}{6}=0$ ✓

Normalize:
\[
\|v_1\|=\sqrt3, \qquad \|v_2\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}=\tfrac{\sqrt6}{3}, \qquad \|v_3\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}.
\]
\[
q_1 = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right), \qquad
q_2 = \left(-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right), \qquad
q_3 = \left(0,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]
\[
\{q_1,q_2,q_3\} = \boxed{\left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right),
\left(-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right),
\left(0,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\right\}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.29 --- Past Paper 2021 Q6
content:
Show that $\{(1,-1,0),(2,-1,-2),(1,-1,-2)\}$ is a basis of
$\mathbb{R}^3$. Find an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ using
the Gram-Schmidt process.

Solution:
Basis check: compute the determinant of the matrix with
these vectors as rows:
\[
\det\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&0\\2&-1&-2\\1&-1&-2\end{bmatrix}
= 1\big((-1)(-2)-(-2)(-1)\big) - (-1)\big((2)(-2)-(-2)(1)\big) + 0
\]
\[
= 1(2-2)+1(-4+2) = 0-2 = -2.
\]
Since $\det = -2 \neq 0$, the vectors are linearly independent and
form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Gram-Schmidt: let $u_1=(1,-1,0)$, $u_2=(2,-1,-2)$,
$u_3=(1,-1,-2)$.
\[
v_1 = u_1 = (1,-1,0), \qquad \langle v_1,v_1 \rangle = 2.
\]
\[
\langle u_2,v_1 \rangle = 2+1+0 = 3.
\]
\[
v_2 = u_2 - \frac{3}{2}v_1 = (2,-1,-2)-\tfrac{3}{2}(1,-1,0)
= \left(\tfrac{1}{2},\ \tfrac{1}{2},\ -2\right),
\qquad \langle v_2,v_2 \rangle = \tfrac{1}{4}+\tfrac{1}{4}+4 = \tfrac{9}{2}.
\]
\[
\langle u_3,v_1 \rangle = 1+1+0 = 2, \qquad
\langle u_3,v_2 \rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}+4 = 4.
\]
\[
v_3 = u_3 - \frac{2}{2}v_1 - \frac{4}{9/2}v_2
= (1,-1,-2) - (1,-1,0) - \tfrac{8}{9}\left(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2},-2\right)
\]
\[
= (0,0,-2) - \left(\tfrac{4}{9},\tfrac{4}{9},-\tfrac{16}{9}\right)
= \left(-\tfrac{4}{9},\ -\tfrac{4}{9},\ -\tfrac{2}{9}\right).
\]
Normalize:
\[
\|v_1\|=\sqrt2, \qquad \|v_2\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{9}{2}}=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt2}, \qquad
\|v_3\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{16}{81}+\tfrac{16}{81}+\tfrac{4}{81}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{36}{81}}=\tfrac{2}{3}.
\]
\[
q_1 = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0\right), \qquad
q_2 = \left(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{6},\tfrac{\sqrt2}{6},-\tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right), \qquad
q_3 = \left(-\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{1}{3}\right).
\]
\[
\{q_1,q_2,q_3\} = \boxed{\left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0\right),
\left(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{6},\tfrac{\sqrt2}{6},-\tfrac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right),
\left(-\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{1}{3}\right)\right\}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 5.30 --- Past Paper 2023 Q6
content:
Show that $\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1),(0,0,1)\}$ is a basis of
$\mathbb{R}^3$. Find an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ using
the Gram-Schmidt process.

Solution:
Basis check: the matrix with these vectors as rows is
upper triangular:
\[
\det\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix} = (1)(1)(1) = 1 \neq 0.
\]
Since the determinant is nonzero, the vectors are linearly
independent and form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Gram-Schmidt: let $u_1=(1,0,1)$, $u_2=(0,1,1)$,
$u_3=(0,0,1)$.
\[
v_1 = u_1 = (1,0,1), \qquad \langle v_1,v_1 \rangle = 2.
\]
\[
\langle u_2,v_1 \rangle = 0+0+1 = 1.
\]
\[
v_2 = u_2 - \frac{1}{2}v_1 = (0,1,1)-\tfrac{1}{2}(1,0,1)
= \left(-\tfrac{1}{2},\ 1,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\right),
\qquad \langle v_2,v_2 \rangle = \tfrac{1}{4}+1+\tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{3}{2}.
\]
\[
\langle u_3,v_1 \rangle = 0+0+1 = 1, \qquad
\langle u_3,v_2 \rangle = 0+0+\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}.
\]
\[
v_3 = u_3 - \frac{1}{2}v_1 - \frac{1/2}{3/2}v_2
= (0,0,1) - \tfrac{1}{2}(1,0,1) - \tfrac{1}{3}\left(-\tfrac{1}{2},1,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)
\]
\[
= \left(-\tfrac{1}{2},0,\tfrac{1}{2}\right) - \left(-\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{6}\right)
= \left(-\tfrac{1}{3},\ -\tfrac{1}{3},\ \tfrac{1}{3}\right).
\]
Normalize:
\[
\|v_1\|=\sqrt2, \qquad \|v_2\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{2}}=\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}, \qquad
\|v_3\|=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{9}+\tfrac{1}{9}+\tfrac{1}{9}}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}.
\]
\[
q_1 = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right), \qquad
q_2 = \left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{2}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right), \qquad
q_3 = \left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right).
\]
\[
\{q_1,q_2,q_3\} = \boxed{\left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0,\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right),
\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{2}{\sqrt6},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\right),
\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)\right\}}
\]

title: {Gram-Schmidt --- Exam Strategy:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Always
content:
Gram-Schmidt --- Exam Strategy:

1. Always compute $v_1=u_1$ first, then find $v_2$ using only
        $v_1$, then $v_3$ using both $v_1$ and $v_2$ ---
        never skip a projection term.
2. Keep $\langle v_i,v_i \rangle$ values recorded as you go;
        they are reused repeatedly in later projection
        coefficients.
3. Always verify orthogonality of each new $v_k$ against all
        previous $v_i$ before moving on --- this catches arithmetic
        errors early.
4. Normalize only at the very end, after the full
        orthogonal basis $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ has been found ---
        normalizing early makes the fractions in later projection
        steps far messier.
5. If the problem also asks to verify the given vectors form a
        basis first, use the determinant test before starting
        Gram-Schmidt.
